messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh was a 50-year-old South Eastern Asian man who had come to therapy after months of feeling unable to settle back into ordinary life following a stalking ordeal that had ended only when the woman who had been following him was finally stopped. He was divorced and worked as a musician, a line of work that once meant late-night gigs, loading gear into unfamiliar venues, and moving easily through crowds, but which had gradually become a source of tension and strain. He described the stalking as having begun in a way that was at first hard to take seriously: repeated appearances by the same woman near places he frequented, then messages and sightings that made it clear she was tracking his movements. Over time he became aware that she could show up where he had no reason to expect anyone to know he would be. That unpredictability changed the shape of his days. He found himself avoiding unfamiliar places because, as he put it, he “couldn’t assess the danger” there. The habit spread quietly into his work life, so that when he was offered a performance in a new bar or asked to rehearse in a studio he had never visited, he felt an immediate tightening and often declined if he could. In the places he still did go, he watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him, scanning faces, hands, and movements with a vigilance that left him distracted and tense. At night the unease became sharper. He said he found it harder to feel safe after dark than during the day, and this was when he checked locks more than once, paused at windows, and listened for sounds outside before trying to sleep.

The memory of the stalking remained fragmented and intensely physical. Minh said there were parts of the event he simply could not remember no matter how hard he tried, especially the sequence of some of the worst encounters. Yet other moments arrived without warning in sharp pieces: the sight of a familiar car slowing near him, the sound of footsteps that seemed to match his own pace, a sudden awareness of being watched while he carried his equipment. At those times, he did not experience the events as distant recollections. He described them as if they were happening again, completely real across all his senses at once. He could feel his chest tighten, hear sounds as clearly as if they were present, and smell the same stale air of a hallway or parking lot that had been part of the original fear. These moments would appear suddenly and then disappear, leaving him unsettled and embarrassed by how quickly he lost his sense of the present. He noticed that a brief flash of memory could come while he was setting up for a set, walking to his car after a gig, or waiting in a dimly lit lot, and the suddenness of it made him feel as though he had no control over when his mind would turn on him.

As the months passed, Minh also began to judge himself in harsh, enduring terms. He often spoke of feeling dead inside, as if the part of him that had once been easygoing, sociable, and responsive had gone flat. He said there were times when he moved through a day and could not feel much beyond fatigue and a dull, muted dread. Alongside that numbness was a conviction that he was a weak person. He was not speaking abstractly; he meant that he saw his own fear, caution, and reduced confidence as proof that he had failed to be the kind of man he believed he should have been. He also carried anger and hurt toward the people and institutions that should have protected him. He felt let down by how long it took for his concerns to be taken seriously and by the sense that the system around him had not been able to keep him safe when he most needed it. That sense of failure remained vivid for him and colored his trust in others. It was part of why he continued to watch people closely and why places that felt unstructured or unfamiliar remained difficult to tolerate.

By the time he sought help, Minh’s world had narrowed. He was still working, but with more hesitation and less ease, and his avoidance had made some professional opportunities harder to accept. He described the decision to come in as being driven less by one single crisis than by the accumulation of nights when he could not relax, moments when a fragment of memory would strike without warning, and the bleak recognition that he felt he was living as a guarded version of himself. What finally brought him to therapy was the fear that he could not keep managing this alone and the hope that he might regain some sense of safety without having to look over his shoulder all the time.
